# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of "Two Years On": Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset

This is a useful follow-up. It does what the earlier papers in this set called for:
- a two-year horizon in a randomised design;
- a second hours measure aimed at unrecorded work;
- a registered test of the meetings hypothesis;
- a check of the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies.

Its conclusions are mostly measured. The main concerns are:
- the Summary conflates two hours measures, which overstates the decline;
- the control offices' "meeting audit" may have contaminated the comparison, which affects how the decline should be read;
- what log-in time actually measures matters a great deal for the mediation result;
- the mediation test is less independent of the exploratory data, and less precise, than presented.

## Arithmetic checks

**These are correct:**
- Output per hour on timesheets: 0.966/0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8%.
- Output per hour on logs: 0.966/0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5%.
- Halden continuers: 34.9/40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4% in hours; 96.8/86.6 = 1.118, so +11.8%.
- Mediation shares: 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.
- Meetings: treated offices fell 3.5 hours and control 0.2, a relative fall of 3.3 hours. That matches the month-six exploratory figure.

**The counter-office cost figure needs its assumption stated.** Restoring contacts handled after an 11.4% fall in output per employee needs about 1/0.886 = 1.129, or roughly 13% more staff. That is consistent with the county's "12% more staff". But 12% more staff handling the same contacts raises *labour* cost per contact by about 12%, not 9%. The 9% figure works only if labour is about three-quarters of total cost per contact. The report should say so.

## 1. The Summary overstates the decline

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log-based figure. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%, as the body of the report correctly says.

| Comparison | Decline |
|---|---|
| 12.5% → 9.8% (timesheets, like-for-like) | about 22% |
| 12.5% → 8.5% (as framed in the Summary) | about 32% |
| Section 5's description | "about a quarter" |

The Summary and Section 5 should use the timesheet comparison for the decline. The log figure should be reported separately, as the 24-month estimate on the stricter measure.

**The decline itself has no confidence interval.** The 9- and 24-month intervals overlap substantially. For the same offices the two estimates are correlated, so a direct test of the difference is needed. The decline may not be distinguishable from zero. "Consistent with some fading" is appropriately hedged. The Summary's flat statement that "the gain has declined" is not.

## 2. The control offices' meeting audit may contaminate the comparison

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their recurring meetings, and their output per hour then rose 4.1%. This is presented as an aside. But it bears directly on the main estimate.

- **It may explain part of the decline.** Treated-relative-to-control falls whenever control offices improve. Part of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% could therefore come from control improvement after month 15, not from fading in the treated offices.
- **It may be a reaction to the trial itself.** The nine-month report, which highlighted meetings, had been published by then. Control offices learning from the trial's own findings is classic contamination.

The report should:
1. split the change in the difference-in-differences estimate into the treated-office trend and the control-office trend;
2. re-estimate the 24-month effect excluding the two auditing control offices, or censoring them at month 15.

If the decline shrinks once this is done, the case for fading becomes weaker. The case against Varga & Holm's novelty argument becomes stronger.

There is also a consistency check worth reporting. The two auditing offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, yet the control mean fell only from 7.2 to 7.0. That implies the other five control offices increased their meeting time by roughly half an hour each, assuming the two auditing offices started near the control mean. If that's right it should be stated; if not, one of the figures needs checking.

## 3. What do log-in hours measure, and what does that mean for the mediation?

Active log-in time on the case-management system captures time spent working on cases, including unclaimed time. That is valuable for detecting unclaimed overtime, the nine-month concern. But it presumably *excludes* meetings, phone calls, paper work and other time off the system. So it is not simply a stricter measure of total hours; it measures a different thing, time on cases.

This matters for the mediation result:

- **Cutting meetings shouldn't directly raise output per case-hour.** The simplest meetings story is that removing low-value time frees hours for casework. That raises output per *total* hour, but not output per *case-hour*.
- **Yet the registered outcome is output per log-measured hour.** If log time excludes meetings, the 47% mediated share must work through some other route, such as fewer interruptions or more focused casework. That is a more interesting finding, but a different one from "removing low-value time".
- **It changes the reading of the hours result.** If log hours exclude meetings, the comparison "logs −11% versus timesheets −12%" partly reflects meeting time being redirected to casework, not just unclaimed work.

The report should state exactly what counts as "active" log-in time. If possible, it should also run the mediation with output per timesheet hour as the outcome.

## 4. The mediation test is weaker than "confirms" suggests

Registering the mediation analysis at month 11 is a genuine improvement. But several issues limit it.

**It may reuse the data that generated the hypothesis.** The text mentions a "larger sample of office-months". If the analysis pools office-months from months 1–24, it includes the months behind the exploratory finding. The confirmatory test would then not be independent of the data that suggested it. The report should restrict the test to months 12–24, or at least report that restriction as a sensitivity analysis.

**Office-months are not independent units.** There are still only 14 offices (7 v 7). A CI of 28% to 66% looks narrow for a proportion mediated with 14 clusters. The report should confirm that inference accounts for clustering, using few-cluster methods.

**The source of baseline meeting data is unclear.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only at month six. Now baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours) appear. If they were retrieved retrospectively from calendar systems, that's fine, but it should be stated.

**Mediator–outcome confounding is acknowledged but understated.** Managers who cut meetings may also differ in other ways that raise output. The Limitations section notes this. The Summary's word "confirms" doesn't fit with that caveat; "supports" would.

Section 3's remark that the hypothesis was "since dismissed as post hoc" is fair as a response to Varga & Holm, but the tone could be more neutral.

## 5. The Halden subset

The figure for the 11 continuing organisations is presented as "an upper bound". That isn't quite right.

- **Selection biases it upward,** as the report says. The organisations are survivors twice over, and 9 of the 23 contacted organisations didn't respond.
- **But the baseline is more than two years old.** With no control group, the comparison picks up any general trend in productivity, new tools and technology, demand and staff changes over that period. These could push the estimate up or down. So it is not strictly a bound in either direction. It is better described as "likely an overestimate for organisations in general".

The baseline of 40.3 hours matches the figure Varga & Holm reported for the 27 organisations with time tracking. The report should confirm it was recomputed for these 11.

The three reversions are informative. In particular, the marketing agency reverted because of client deadlines, which suggests coverage-type constraints can arise in nominally discretionary sectors. That supports the Varden authors' point that what matters is the role, not the sector.

## 6. Still missing from the Varden results

- **Cost.** Output per FTE is −3.4% at full pay, plus whatever overtime is claimed. Labour cost per case has therefore risen, by something like 3.5% or more. Two years in, a cost per case closed comparison, treated versus control, would make the policy implication clear.
- **Uncertainty for secondary outcomes.** Appeal overturns (3.2% v 3.0%), resignations and sick days are still reported without CIs or difference-in-differences estimates.
- **Small-cluster inference.** The 24-month CIs should use the same few-cluster methods I suggested at nine months.

## 7. How this bears on the earlier papers

**Varga & Holm.** The rebuttal is fair. Varden at 24 months meets almost all of their own recommended standards: records, actual hours, randomisation, at least 18 months, and no withdrawals in the case-processing arm. It still finds a gain that excludes zero. Two qualifications:
- Their extrapolation was of self-reported energy, in a different population, not of output.
- The month-ten zero point was itself an arithmetic slip; the straight-line extrapolation reaches zero around month nine.

The point stands regardless.

**The meta-analysis.** The finding that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours directly answers the concern I raised about the meta-analysis's duration section. The meta-analysis should be corrected. "Cannot speak to decay" is slightly strong; the four studies are weak evidence rather than none.

**Varden's own counter-office result.** The counter arm ended at month 12 with longer waits and higher costs. That confirms the nine-month finding on coverage-bound work.

**Authorship.** Including a Halden author (Okafor) is reasonable given the data access. It should be noted as a disclosure, since the report adjudicates criticism of that author's own working paper.

## Overall

This is the best evidence in the series. It suggests a durable per-hour gain in discretionary public-sector casework of roughly 8–10%, with output per employee slightly below control. It also supports the meetings mechanism, plausibly, though not conclusively.

The changes I'd ask for:
1. use the like-for-like decline (12.5% → 9.8%) in the Summary, with a CI on the change;
2. separate treated and control trends, and test sensitivity to the two auditing control offices;
3. define log-in time and rerun the mediation on timesheet hours;
4. restrict the mediation test to post-registration data, with few-cluster inference;
5. describe the Halden figure as a likely overestimate rather than an upper bound;
6. add a cost-per-case comparison.

The trial's own design limitation is the most important open question. Since no arm reorganised without reducing hours, it can't say whether the meetings gain requires the hours cut. A future trial with a meetings-only arm would answer it.
